WASHINGTON (CNN) -- As President Obama approaches day 100 of his administration, some in Washington caution that the torture tug-of-war could be a costly distraction. Leg restraints await detainees at Guantanamo Bay in this 2006 photo. Earlier this month, the Obama administration released four Bush-era memos detailing "enhanced interrogations" of suspected al Qaeda members. Now, the White House is reviewing former Vice President Dick Cheney's request to make more memos public. Two weeks before Obama released any memos, Cheney submitted a request to the National Archives calling for the release of other documents. He says that what he requested will prove that the Bush interrogation tactics -- which critics have called a torture program -- worked. "I haven't talked about it, but I know specifically of reports that I read, that I saw, that lay out what we learned through the interrogation process and what the consequences were for the country," Cheney said in an interview with Fox News last week. The White House is signaling that not only is it considering honoring Cheney's request, it may go even further. "I think the president, as you know, is a big believer in transparency," White House press secretary Robert Gibbs said Sunday on NBC's "Meet the Press." "I think one of the things that will have to be examined is whether there are additional memos that have to be released that give a broader picture of what's gone on in enhanced interrogation techniques." The almost daily revelations are dividing Democrats between those calling for full disclosure and those urging caution. "We don't just turn the page without reading it. We want to make sure what the mistakes were so that the Obama administration doesn't make these mistakes," Sen. Patrick Leahy, D-Vermont. said Sunday. But Sen. Dianne Feinstein, D-California, warned Sunday against moving to quickly. "We need to find these things out, and we need to do it in a way that's calm and deliberative and professional, because I think all of this, on the front burner, before the public, does harm our intelligence gathering, it does harm America's position in the world," she said on CNN's "State of the Union." Across the aisle, Republicans are insisting the Justice Department drop any investigation of Bush administration officials who authorized harsh interrogations. "I think that would be a stab in the back. I think he has already demoralized the CIA, put them in a CYA mode," Sen. Kit Bond, R-Missouri, said Sunday on Fox News. Arizona Sen. John McCain, the former Republican presidential candidate, said prosecuting those who gave legal advice is wrong. "I don't think those memos should have been released, but the fundamental point now is whether to prosecute people who gave the president, in my view, legitimate advice, even though it was wrong," he said.  "We should not be prosecuting people who gave legal advice. It's wrong to do that to them, and it sets a terrible precedent for the future." Rep. Pete Hoekstra of Michigan, the top Republican on the House Intelligence Committee, and House Minority Leader John Boehner of Ohio are calling on the White House to release a list of who was briefed about the interrogation programs. "Congress and the American people deserve a full and complete set of facts about what information was yielded by CIA's interrogation program, and they deserve to know which of their representatives in Congress were briefed about these techniques and the extent of those briefings," Boehner said in a statement Monday. "To date, the administration has fallen short in providing this information. ... The American people have been provided an incomplete picture of exactly what intelligence was made available by the interrogation program," he said. But Connecticut Sen. Joe Lieberman, a Democrat-turned-independent, said the whole debate over the memos is "moot." "What do we gain, first, by releasing the memos; but, secondly, what do we gain from indicting lawyers for their opinions, if that is a possibility here? ... It will poison the water here in Washington. It will achieve nothing. It will make it harder for President Obama to do some of the big things he wants to do for the country," he said.

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — As President Barack Obama approaches the 100-day milestone of his administration, political observers in Washington caution that the intensifying debate over interrogation practices threatens to become a costly distraction. (A 2006 photograph depicting leg restraints awaiting detainees at Guantanamo Bay underscores the enduring gravity of the issue.)

Two weeks prior to the administration's initial release, Cheney submitted a formal request to the National Archives for the disclosure of complementary records. He maintains that these documents will prove that the Bush administration’s interrogation tactics—denounced by critics as a state-sanctioned torture program—were effective. 

"I haven't talked about it, but I know specifically of reports that I read, that I saw, that lay out what we learned through the interrogation process and what the consequences were for the country," Cheney stated during an interview with Fox News.

The White House has signaled a willingness not only to honor Cheney’s request, but potentially to expand the scope of disclosure even further. 

"I think the president, as you know, is a big believer in transparency," White House Press Secretary Robert Gibbs remarked on NBC's *Meet the Press*. "I think one of the things that will have to be examined is whether there are additional memos that have to be released that give a broader picture of what's gone on in enhanced interrogation techniques."

The steady stream of revelations is fracturing Democrats between advocates for full transparency and proponents of strategic restraint. 

"We don't just turn the page without reading it. We want to make sure what the mistakes were so that the Obama administration doesn't make these mistakes," said Senator Patrick Leahy, D-Vermont. 

Conversely, Senator Dianne Feinstein, D-California, warned against moving precipitously. "We need to find these things out, and we need to do it in a way that's calm and deliberative and professional, because I think all of this, on the front burner, before the public, does harm our intelligence gathering, it does harm America's position in the world," she observed on CNN’s *State of the Union*.

Across the aisle, Republicans are demanding that the Justice Department refrain from initiating any criminal investigation into Bush administration officials who authorized the harsh interrogations. 

"I think that would be a stab in the back. I think he has already demoralized the CIA, put them in a CYA mode," Senator Kit Bond, R-Missouri, asserted on Fox News.

Senator John McCain, R-Arizona, the former Republican presidential nominee, similarly argued that prosecuting legal advisors sets a dangerous precedent. "I don't think those memos should have been released, but the fundamental point now is whether to prosecute people who gave the president, in my view, legitimate advice, even though it was wrong," McCain said. "We should not be prosecuting people who gave legal advice. It's wrong to do that to them, and it sets a terrible precedent for the future."

Meanwhile, Representative Pete Hoekstra of Michigan, the ranking Republican on the House Intelligence Committee, alongside House Minority Leader John Boehner of Ohio, are calling on the White House to release a comprehensive list of lawmakers who were briefed on the interrogation programs. 

"Congress and the American people deserve a full and complete set of facts about what information was yielded by CIA's interrogation program, and they deserve to know which of their representatives in Congress were briefed about these techniques and the extent of those briefings," Boehner said in a statement. "To date, the administration has fallen short in providing this information. ... The American people have been provided an incomplete picture of exactly what intelligence was made available by the interrogation program."

However, Senator Joe Lieberman, an independent from Connecticut, characterized the overarching debate over the memos as entirely moot. 

"What do we gain, first, by releasing the memos; but, secondly, what do we gain from indicting lawyers for their opinions, if that is a possibility here? ... It will poison the water here in Washington. It will achieve nothing. It will make it harder for President Obama to do some of the big things he wants to do for the country," Lieberman warned.

**Cheney demands release of 'interrogation success' memos as political battle escalates**

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — A fierce political battle over the legacy of the Bush administration's counterterrorism policies intensified Tuesday, as former Vice President Dick Cheney demanded the Obama administration declassify additional documents that he claims prove "enhanced interrogation techniques" saved American lives.

Cheney’s public offensive follows President Barack Obama’s decision last week to release four controversial Justice Department legal memos. Written during the Bush presidency, the documents provided detailed legal justifications for harsh CIA interrogation tactics—including waterboarding, sleep deprivation, and stress positions—used against high-value al Qaeda suspects.

Speaking in a televised interview, Cheney accused the current administration of telling only "half the story" by releasing the legal framework for the techniques without showing the intelligence yield they produced.

"I have formally asked the CIA to declassify two specific memos," Cheney said. "One of the reasons I think it's important to be released is because the public ought to know what we accomplished... They show directly the intelligence that was gathered as a result of using those techniques."

Cheney argued that the release of the legal memos endangered national security by revealing intelligence tactics to foreign adversaries while ignoring the context of the post-September 11 environment.

**The White House defends transparency**

The White House pushed back firmly against Cheney’s assertions, maintaining that President Obama’s decision to release the documents was about restoring the rule of law and transparency, not settling political scores.

During a visit to CIA headquarters in Langley, Virginia, on Monday, President Obama sought to reassure intelligence officers while standing by his decision to end the harsh practices and make the legal memos public.

"I know that the last few days have been extraordinarily difficult," Obama told CIA employees. "Do not be discouraged by what’s happened over the last few days. Calculate it as part of the price of living in a democracy."

Administration officials have repeatedly argued that the techniques damaged America's moral standing in the world and served as a potent recruiting tool for terrorist groups. Furthermore, Obama administration officials contend that traditional, non-coercive interrogation methods are equally, if not more, effective.

Responding to Cheney's demands, White House Press Secretary Robert Gibbs said the CIA is currently reviewing the former vice president's request to declassify the additional documents through standard procedures. However, Gibbs expressed skepticism regarding Cheney's claims that the techniques were essential to keeping the country safe.

"It is the belief of the president, the Director of National Intelligence, and the Director of the CIA that we can keep this country safe without compromising our values," Gibbs told reporters.

Obama has also assured CIA operatives who carried out the interrogations that they will not face criminal prosecution, provided they acted in good-faith reliance on the legal guidance provided by the Bush Justice Department at the time.

**Partisan divide in Congress**

The clash between the current and former administrations has reignited a bitter partisan debate on Capitol Hill.

Congressional Democrats praised the release of the memos and called for further scrutiny into how the policies were formulated. Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Patrick Leahy, D-Vermont, renewed his call for a nonpartisan "truth commission" to investigate allegations of abuse.

"The American people deserve to know what was done in their name," Leahy said. "Transparency is the first step toward restoring our credibility on human rights."

Key Senate Democrats, including Intelligence Committee Chairwoman Dianne Feinstein, D-California, argued that releasing the full truth is vital to ensuring the nation does not repeat the mistakes of the past.

Republicans, however, largely rallied behind Cheney, accusing the Obama administration of playing politics with national security and throwing intelligence officers under the bus.

Minority Leader Mitch McConnell, R-Kentucky, warned that releasing the memos provided a "roadmap" for future terrorists seeking to train against U.S. interrogation methods.

"Publishing these memos sends a chilling signal to the men and women who keep us safe," McConnell said on the Senate floor. "It tells them that the legal advice they rely on today could be published and criticized by the next administration tomorrow."

Rep. Peter King, R-New York, the ranking member on the House Homeland Security Committee, echoed Cheney’s demands, calling on the White House to release all relevant intelligence reports to give the public a complete picture.

"If the president is going to selectively release documents to satisfy his political base, then he owes it to the American people to release the documents that show how many lives were saved by these operations," King said.

As the CIA reviews Cheney's request to declassify the remaining documents, the debate highlights a fundamental divide in Washington over how the nation should balance national security with American values in a post-9/11 world.

**WASHINGTON** — Former Vice President Dick Cheney has intensified his defense of Bush-era counterterrorism policies, publicly demanding that the Obama administration declassify secret CIA documents that he claims demonstrate the effectiveness of harsh interrogation techniques. 

Cheney’s request has ignited a fierce political battle on Capitol Hill, splitting lawmakers over national security, government transparency, and the legacy of the post-9/11 "War on Terror."

Speaking in a televised interview, Cheney argued that the administration engaged in selective transparency last week when it released four previously classified Department of Justice legal memos. Those documents detailed controversial interrogation methods approved under the Bush administration, including sleep deprivation, stress positions, and waterboarding.

Cheney asserted that by releasing only the legal justifications for the techniques without the accompanying reports detailing the intelligence gained, the Obama administration presented a skewed narrative to the American public.

"I know specifically of at least two documents that are still classified that detail the particular success we had with these programs," Cheney said. "I've formally asked the CIA to declassify them, and I hope the administration will agree to do so, because I think it's important for the American public to see the whole story."

Cheney maintained that the coercive methods—which critics, human rights groups, and many international legal experts label as torture—were vital in extracting actionable intelligence that prevented subsequent attacks and saved thousands of lives.

### Capitol Hill Reacts

Cheney’s public mandate promptly drew sharp, polarized reactions from members of Congress.

**Democratic Response:**
Congressional Democrats strongly pushed back against Cheney's comments, backing President Barack Obama’s decision to ban the techniques and defend the release of the legal memos. 

Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid (D-Nev.) rejected Cheney's assertions, arguing that national security is not served by defending practices that violate international law. 

"Vice President Cheney's continued defense of torture is both predictable and wrong," Reid told reporters. "The former vice president seems more interested in defending the past administration's deeply flawed policies than in helping the country move forward."

Members of the Senate Intelligence Committee, which is currently conducting its own bipartisan investigation into the CIA program, cautioned against taking Cheney's claims at face value. Democratic lawmakers argued that intelligence cited as "success stories" by proponents of harsh interrogations was either obtained prior to the use of coercive methods or could have been secured using standard, non-coercive police and military questioning tactics.

**Republican Response:**
Conversely, Capitol Hill Republicans largely rallied to Cheney’s side, accusing the Obama administration of playing politics with national security and endangering intelligence operatives by releasing the legal memos in the first place.

Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) supported Cheney’s call for further declassification, arguing that if the public is to see the methods used, they should also see the results.

"If the administration is going to release documents that outline the techniques, it ought to release the documents that show what was accomplished as a result of using those techniques," McConnell said. "To release one without the other gives the public an incomplete and biased picture."

House Minority Leader John Boehner (R-Ohio) echoed those sentiments, stating that the release of the legal memos set a dangerous precedent, but agreed that full transparency regarding the intelligence yield was now necessary to balance the record.

### White House and CIA Position

The White House acknowledged Cheney's request, noting that any decision regarding the declassification of additional documents rests with the intelligence community. President Obama has maintained that while he believes the interrogation techniques were a mistake and contrary to American values, he wishes to "look forward, not backward" regarding the policies of the previous administration.

A CIA spokesperson confirmed that the agency had received Cheney's request to review the classified documents for potential public release, stating that the request would be processed through standard agency channels.

As the debate continues to unfold, the feud highlights a deep and persistent ideological divide in Washington over the balance between national security tactics and moral principles—a debate that shows no signs of dissipating.

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — As President Barack Obama prepares to mark his 100th day in office this week, the White House was hoping to showcase a sweeping domestic agenda dominated by economic recovery, healthcare reform, and a historic stimulus package. 

Instead, the nation’s capital is consumed by a bitter, escalating battle over the past.

The Obama administration’s decision earlier this month to release four controversial Justice Department legal memos detailing the CIA’s use of harsh interrogation techniques—including waterboarding, sleep deprivation, and stress positions—has ignited a political firestorm. Now, as partisan warfare over the Bush-era "torture memos" intensifies, allies and critics alike are questioning whether the controversy threatens to derail the President’s legislative momentum at a critical juncture.

For the White House, the release was meant to fulfill a campaign promise of government transparency while drawing a clear line under the previous administration's counterterrorism policies. But the move has pleased neither side. Progressive Democrats are demanding special prosecutors to investigate former Bush administration officials, while Republicans accuse the White House of compromising national security to appease its political base.

Press Secretary Robert Gibbs spent much of Monday’s press briefing attempting to steer the conversation back to the administration’s core agenda, reinforcing President Obama’s desire to avoid a protracted legal reckoning over the past.

"The President believes we need to look forward, not backward," Gibbs told reporters. "He made a decision based on the legal circumstances surrounding the court order and his commitment to transparency. But the President’s primary focus—and the focus of this administration—remains on fixing a generational economic crisis, reforming healthcare, and keeping the American people safe."

Yet, looking forward is proving difficult when high-profile figures from the previous administration are aggressively fighting back. 

Former Vice President Dick Cheney has emerged as the chief defender of the CIA’s practices, launching an unprecedented media offensive against the new administration. In a series of interviews and public requests, Cheney demanded that the Obama administration declassify additional CIA documents that he claims prove the interrogations successfully thwarted terror plots and saved American lives.

"The intelligence reports show that the enhanced interrogation techniques were highly effective," Cheney said in an interview detailing his formal request to the National Archives. "Releasing the legal memos describing the techniques, while withholding the internal memos that document their success, gives the public a completely distorted picture. Releasing one without the other does a grave disservice to the American people and the men and women who protected this country after 9/11."

The intelligence debate has created a complex political minefield for moderate lawmakers and national security hawks, many of whom worry the controversy will paralyze Congress just as major legislation is moving through Capitol Hill.

Senator John McCain (R-AZ), a former prisoner of war who long opposed the Bush administration’s use of coercive interrogations, found himself caught between his principled opposition to waterboarding and his deep concern over the political turn the debate has taken.

**Debate Deepens Over Bush-Era CIA Interrogations as Calls for Prosecution Split Washington**

**WASHINGTON** — A fierce debate has re-emerged in the nation’s capital over the CIA’s post-9/11 interrogation program, as lawmakers, legal experts, and human rights advocates clash over whether government officials who authorized brutal interrogation techniques should face criminal prosecution.

The controversy follows the recent release of previously classified Department of Justice memos detailing the use of "enhanced interrogation techniques" (EITs)—including waterboarding, sleep deprivation, stress positions, and wall-slamming—against suspected high-value detainees held in secret overseas facilities.

The revelations have reignited a fundamental question that has divided Washington for years: Does upholding the rule of law require prosecuting those who authorized and implemented methods widely condemned as torture, or would doing so dangerously politicize national security decisions made in the wake of the country's worst terrorist attack?

### The Case for Prosecution

Human rights groups, international legal experts, and many progressive lawmakers argue that failing to hold officials accountable sets a dangerous precedent. They contend that techniques like waterboarding explicitly violate both U.S. federal law and international treaties, such as the United Nations Convention Against Torture and the Geneva Conventions.

"No nation can maintain moral authority or claim to uphold the rule of law if it grants immunity to high-ranking officials who authorize torture," said Laura Pitter, a senior counterterrorism advisor at a prominent human rights organization. "Looking the other way because it is politically inconvenient undermines our legal system and signals to the rest of the world that human rights protections are conditional."

Proponents of prosecution argue that a formal legal review—potentially targeting top architects of the policy within the Bush administration's Justice Department and CIA—is necessary to ensure that such practices are never repeated. 

### The Defense: National Security and Legal Coverage

Defenders of the program, including former senior CIA officials and members of the Bush administration, vigorously push back against calls for prosecution. They maintain that the techniques were executed in good faith, relied on legal opinions provided by the Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel (OLC), and were crucial in extracting actionable intelligence that prevented subsequent terrorist attacks.

Former Vice President Dick Cheney and other key figures have argued that the methods were necessary during a time of crisis and that criminalizing policy disagreements sets a harmful precedent.

"The men and women of the CIA were asked to do a difficult job under extraordinary circumstances to keep this country safe," said a former high-ranking CIA officer speaking on the condition of anonymity. "They sought legal guidance before acting, and they were told their actions were lawful. To now turn around and prosecute intelligence officers or their leaders for political reasons will have a chilling effect on the entire national security enterprise."

Critics of prosecution also warn that launching high-profile criminal investigations into a previous administration risks turning intelligence policy into a partisan weapon, distracting from current national security priorities.

### The Political Dilemma

The debate presents a significant dilemma for the White House and the Department of Justice. While President Barack Obama has officially banned the use of harsh interrogation techniques via executive order, his administration has expressed reluctance to pursue criminal charges against former officials, emphasizing a desire to "look forward, not backward."

However, Attorney General Eric Holder faces growing pressure from within his own party and from international bodies to appoint a special prosecutor to review potential criminal acts. While the DOJ has signaled that CIA operatives who acted in good faith within the boundaries of the legal memos should not be prosecuted, the question of whether those who *drafted* the legal authorizations should face scrutiny remains unanswered.

As Congressional committees continue their own investigations into the effectiveness and morality of the CIA program, Washington remains deeply divided. Whether the issue ends in courtroom prosecutions, a truth commission, or political stalemate, the debate over Bush-era interrogations continues to test the boundaries of executive power, accountability, and the American justice system.
